title: F9 – Corporate strategy: diversification, vertical integration and internationalization
source: Vorschau: Die Folien zu Corporate Strategy liegen noch nicht im Ordner. Zusammenfassung der Standard-Frameworks (Johnson, Whittington et al., Exploring Strategy; Yip; Ghemawat), die in der Klausur Dez. 2023 (Fragen 4 und 5) verlangt wurden.

blocks.text: Corporate strategy answers “where to compete?”: the scope of the organization – which products and markets (diversification), which activities of the value system (vertical integration) and which countries (internationalization) – and how to allocate resources across businesses.
Every scope decision should pass two tests: does the industry offer value to capture (external analysis), and are the firm's resources and capabilities valuable there (VRIO travels or not – Dyson)?
Each move has trade-offs: more control and margin vs. less flexibility, more capital, more coordination – and possible conflicts with the organization's identity.
Market penetration: existing products, existing markets (gain share).
Product development: new products for existing markets.
Market development: existing products for new markets (new segments or countries – internationalization).

Diversification: new products for new markets – related (shares resources, capabilities or customers with the core business → synergies, economies of scope) or unrelated/conglomerate (financial logic, few synergies).
Synergy test: is the new business worth more inside the group than outside? Link with F8 – spanning categories may cost an illegitimacy discount.

Backward integration: moving upstream into the activities of suppliers (a supermarket producing its own milk). Forward integration: moving downstream into the activities of buyers/distributors (a brand opening its own stores).
Benefits:
children: Control over quality, supply security and timing of key inputs
Capture the margin of the integrated stage
Reduce the bargaining power of suppliers or buyers (Five Forces)
Protect and coordinate distinctive resources (know-how, data, customer relationship)
Create entry barriers (formal control of supply or distribution)

blocks.text: Costs and risks:
children: Capital requirements and fixed costs; less flexibility to switch to better or cheaper partners
Capabilities may not fit the new activity (a different business to manage)
Coordination and bureaucracy costs; loss of the market's incentive effects
For labour-intensive stages: employment obligations (salaries, social security) instead of flexible contracts
Possible conflict with identity and with partners who become competitors

blocks.text: Make or buy: integrate when transaction costs of using the market are high – specific assets, high uncertainty, frequent transactions, risk of opportunism – and when the activity is strategically core. Otherwise outsource. Intermediate options: long-term contracts, alliances, joint ventures, minority stakes, franchising.
Market drivers: similar customer needs and tastes across countries, global customers, transferable marketing (e.g. growing awareness of mental health worldwide).
Cost drivers: economies of scale and learning, country-specific cost advantages, high development costs that need large markets (digital products: near-zero marginal cost per extra user).
Government drivers: trade policies, regulation, standards, data protection (e.g. GDPR in Europe), host-government policies – can favour or hinder.
Competitive drivers: interdependence between countries, global competitors already present, need to follow rivals or customers abroad.
Firm-level test: are the resources and capabilities transferable and still VRIO abroad (brand, content, community, know-how)? Do they need local adaptation (language, culture, partners)?

CAGE distance (Ghemawat): Cultural (language, religion, norms), Administrative (institutions, regulation, trade agreements), Geographic (physical distance, time zones), Economic (income levels, costs, infrastructure). Greater distance → more adaptation and risk.
Entry modes, from low to high commitment and control: exporting / digital distribution, licensing and franchising, alliances and joint ventures, wholly owned subsidiaries (greenfield or acquisition).
Global integration vs local responsiveness: standardize to exploit scale (global strategy) or adapt to local needs (multidomestic) – or combine (transnational).
Entering activities of the firm's suppliers (upstream).
Entering activities of the firm's buyers or distributors (downstream).
Moving into businesses that share resources, capabilities or customers with the core.
Market, cost, government and competitive drivers that push an industry towards global strategies.
Cultural, administrative, geographic and economic distance between countries.

sections.heading: Further thinking: how to answer a corporate-strategy question

blocks.text: Vertical integration: name the concrete stage (e.g. “Insight Timer employs its teachers” = backward; “Insight Timer opens meditation studios” = forward), then argue benefits vs costs with the Five Forces (bargaining power) and VRIO (does it protect a distinctive resource?), and conclude on the consequences for the business model and identity.
Internationalization: motives = drivers (market, cost, government, competitive) applied to the case; consistency = which resources travel (VRIO abroad, CAGE distance) and which need adaptation.
